Learning objectives

This guide covers the modalities used to image the respiratory tract — plain chest radiography (CXR), computed tomography (CT), CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA), ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scanning, PET/CT, and point-of-care ultrasound — and walks through how each is used to build (or exclude) a diagnosis. It is not an exhaustive radiology survey; instead, it emphasizes the patterns a clinician needs to recognize at the bedside: distinguishing heart failure from pneumonia, staging sarcoidosis, recognizing pneumothorax (including the emergency of tension pneumothorax), interpreting the major diffuse interstitial lung disease patterns on CT, and knowing when to reach for V/Q scanning, CTPA, or ultrasound.

By the end of this guide, you should be able to:

  • Describe the importance of chest radiography in diagnosis, and use a systematic (ABCDEF) approach to reading a CXR.
  • Recognize and explain the significance of consolidations, interstitial infiltrates, and signs of pleural effusion or pneumothorax on CXR.
  • Describe the roles of CT scanning, CT angiography, PET/CT scanning, ventilation/perfusion scanning, and ultrasound in diagnosing respiratory disease.
  • Differentiate the chest x-ray findings of cardiogenic pulmonary edema from those of pneumonia, and recognize the classic patterns of atypical pneumonia, COPD, sarcoidosis, pneumothorax, and the major diffuse parenchymal lung diseases on CT.

CXR fundamentals: airspace, interstitial, and pleural disease

Chest radiography is the essential first study in respiratory diagnosis. It visualizes the lower respiratory tract, the size and contour of the heart, the great vessels (aorta, pulmonary arteries and veins), the bones, and any implanted devices (pacemakers, catheters, lines, and tubes). Because a radiologist may not be immediately available when an urgent diagnosis is needed, every clinician should be comfortable reading a CXR using a systematic approach — commonly taught as the ABCDEF method: Airway, Bones and breast shadows, Cardiac silhouette and mediastinum, Diaphragm and upper abdomen, Equipment (lines, tubes, devices), and Fields of the lungs. This ensures that findings outside the lung fields — a displaced trachea, a rib fracture, an enlarged heart, a malpositioned catheter — are not missed while focusing on the parenchyma.

Reading the lung fields themselves is often the hardest skill to learn in chest radiography, because many different diseases share overlapping appearances (most reflect an increase in lung fluid of one kind or another). It helps enormously to first sort any abnormality into one of three broad categories:

1. Airspace disease and consolidation

Normal, air-filled lung is radiolucent (dark) on CXR. When the alveoli themselves fill with material that absorbs x-rays more than air — cells, protein, water, pus, blood, or transudate — the film shows opacification (increased whiteness) known as pulmonary consolidation. Consolidation has a classic "fluffy," "cloud-like" quality, as though the whiteness had been filled in with an airbrush, and it can be confluent throughout the lung or limited to one or more lobes. "Consolidation" is a nonspecific descriptive term: the material filling the alveoli can come from pneumonia, cardiogenic pulmonary edema, pulmonary hemorrhage, aspiration, or (less commonly) noninfectious inflammatory disease.

2. Interstitial disease

"Interstitial disease" describes a group of disorders in which fluid or fibrosis accumulates in the connective-tissue scaffolding between the alveoli and terminal bronchioles, rather than filling the alveolar spaces themselves. Interstitial disease often begins with inflammation and may progress to scarring/fibrosis, impairing gas exchange. On CXR it produces several recognizable patterns:

  • Honeycombing (cysts and fibrosis) — chronic inflammation, including usual interstitial pneumonia.
  • Linear opacities — linear streaks from interstitial thickening, common in pulmonary edema and some (especially viral) pneumonias.
  • Miliary opacities — tiny nodules scattered throughout the lung, seen in tuberculosis, fungal infection, metastatic cancer, sarcoidosis, and pneumoconiosis.
  • Nodules (round white spots) — tumors, TB.
  • Reticular opacities — curvilinear areas of opacity without discrete nodules, seen in pulmonary edema, pulmonary fibrosis, and silicosis.
Clinical pearlPulmonary edema from congestive heart failure can present as either consolidation or an interstitial pattern — sometimes both at once — because the excess fluid can accumulate in the alveoli, the interstitium, or both simultaneously as pressures rise.

3. Pleural disease

The pleural space is normally a thin potential space containing little or no fluid or air. Two common pleural disorders are visible on CXR:

  • A pleural effusion is an accumulation of excess fluid in the pleural space, appearing radiopaque relative to lung. It is most easily seen on an erect film at the costophrenic angles — the lowest part of the pleural space — where fluid often produces a classic upward-curving meniscus.
  • A pneumothorax is free air within the pleural space. The visceral pleural edge appears as a sharp white line, with the space peripheral to it appearing truly radiolucent (black) because it lacks the normal branching vascular markings of aerated lung. A large pneumothorax is obvious; a small one may be subtle and easy to confuse with an overlying rib margin.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
A patient's chest x-ray shows confluent, fluffy, airbrush-like whiteness filling the right middle lobe, obscuring the normal branching vascular markings there. Which category of lung pathology does this represent?
AInterstitial disease
BPleural disease
CAirspace disease (consolidation)
DNormal aeration
EMediastinal mass
Explanation: Fluid or cells filling the alveoli themselves (rather than the interstitium) displace air and produce confluent, fluffy opacification — consolidation, the radiographic signature of airspace disease. Causes include pneumonia, pulmonary edema, hemorrhage, and aspiration. This differs from interstitial disease, in which fluid or fibrosis thickens the tissue between alveoli and produces linear, nodular, or honeycomb patterns rather than confluent whiteness.
Exam-style question
Which CXR pattern is most characteristic of interstitial (rather than airspace) lung disease?
AAir bronchograms within a lobar opacity
BA meniscus-shaped opacity at the costophrenic angle
CA visceral pleural line with absent lung markings peripheral to it
DDiffuse whiteout of a hemithorax with tracheal shift toward the opacity
EHoneycombing, reticular markings, or diffuse fine linear/nodular opacities
Explanation: Interstitial disease reflects fluid or fibrosis in the tissue scaffolding between alveoli rather than filling of the alveoli themselves, and so it appears as honeycombing (cystic change with fibrosis), reticular (net-like) opacities, linear streaks, miliary nodules, or discrete nodules — never as confluent airspace whiteness. Air bronchograms and lobar consolidation reflect airspace disease; a meniscus at the costophrenic angle is pleural effusion; an absent-lung-marking peripheral zone with a visible pleural line is pneumothorax; whiteout with tracheal shift toward the opacity suggests volume loss (atelectasis) rather than an interstitial pattern.

Heart failure vs. pneumonia on chest x-ray

One of the most common — and most difficult — distinctions a student must learn to make on CXR is separating cardiogenic pulmonary edema (heart failure) from pneumonia, because both can produce consolidation, and both can be accompanied by pleural fluid. The key is to look for a constellation of secondary signs of elevated cardiac filling pressure and volume overload, which point toward heart failure: increased vascular pedicle width, redistribution of pulmonary blood flow, Kerley B lines, and an enlarged cardiac silhouette.

Staging cardiogenic pulmonary edema

As left heart filling pressure (pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, PCWP) rises, the radiographic findings of heart failure progress through three recognizable stages:

StageApprox. PCWPRadiographic findings
Stage 1 — Redistribution13–18 mmHgRedistribution of pulmonary blood flow (cephalization), cardiomegaly, broadened vascular pedicle
Stage 2 — Interstitial edema18–25 mmHgKerley lines, peribronchial cuffing, hazy loss of definition of vessels (perihilar haze), thickened interlobar fissure
Stage 3 — Alveolar edema>25 mmHgConsolidation, air bronchograms, "cottonwool" appearance, pleural effusion

Redistribution (cephalization) and the artery-to-bronchus ratio

On a normal, erect chest film, gravity keeps more blood volume in the lung bases, so the pulmonary vessels supplying the upper lung fields are normally smaller and fewer than those supplying the bases. However, the pulmonary vascular bed has substantial reserve capacity: as venous pressure rises, previously non-perfused upper-lobe vessels are recruited and open, and already-perfused vessels distend — producing redistribution of blood flow to the upper zones, sometimes called cephalization. This is best appreciated by comparing the diameter of the pulmonary artery to its accompanying bronchus at different levels: normally this ratio is about 0.85 in the upper lobes, roughly 1.0 at the hilum, and about 1.35 in the lower lobes. When redistribution occurs, the upper- and middle-lobe artery-to-bronchus ratio increases toward or beyond the normal hilar/basal values.

Kerley B lines and peribronchial cuffing

As pressures climb further, fluid leaks from the pulmonary capillaries into the surrounding interstitium — interstitial edema. Fluid that accumulates in the peripheral interlobular septa produces Kerley B lines: short (1–2 cm), horizontal lines seen at the lung periphery near the costophrenic angles, oriented perpendicular to the pleura. Fluid that instead accumulates in the central peribronchovascular interstitium thickens the walls of the bronchi in cross-section (peribronchial cuffing) and blurs the normally sharp margins of the hilar vessels, producing a hazy, indistinct appearance called perihilar haze.

Alveolar edema: the full-blown picture, and its resolution with treatment

At the most advanced stage, fluid floods the alveoli themselves, producing frank consolidation. A classic film demonstrating decompensated heart failure at this stage shows: alveolar edema with perihilar consolidation and air bronchograms (small lucent airways outlined by surrounding opacified alveoli), pleural fluid, a prominent azygos vein, an increased vascular pedicle width, and an enlarged cardiac silhouette — all occurring together.

Contrast: a straightforward bacterial (lobar) pneumonia

By contrast, a right lobar pneumonia shows a very different overall picture even though it also produces consolidation: the heart size is normal, the vascular pedicle is normal, and there are no Kerley B lines, no vascular redistribution, and no pleural effusion. The absence of these secondary signs of volume overload and elevated filling pressure — combined with the more unilateral, lobar distribution of the opacity — helps separate a primary pneumonia from cardiogenic pulmonary edema, even though both share the underlying finding of consolidation.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
On a standing chest film, which finding indicates redistribution (cephalization) of pulmonary blood flow, an early sign of elevated left-heart filling pressure?
AKerley B lines at the costophrenic angles
BAn artery-to-bronchus diameter ratio in the upper lobes that is increased toward or beyond that seen at the hila, rather than the normal ~0.85 ratio
CA sharp white visceral pleural line with radiolucency peripheral to it
DA meniscus-shaped opacity at the costophrenic angle
ELoss of the retrosternal airspace on the lateral view
Explanation: Normally, gravity keeps more blood flow (and larger vessels) in the lung bases when a patient stands, so the upper-lobe artery-to-bronchus ratio is only about 0.85, rising to about 1.0 at the hilum and 1.35 at the bases. As left atrial/pulmonary venous pressure rises (Stage 1 CHF, PCWP roughly 13–18 mmHg), the vascular reserve capacity in the upper zones opens and distends, so upper-lobe vessels enlarge relative to their accompanying bronchi — cephalization/redistribution. This precedes interstitial edema (Kerley lines, PCWP ~18–25) and alveolar edema (consolidation, air bronchograms, PCWP >25), which are later stages.
Exam-style question
A 62-year-old with acute dyspnea has a CXR showing an enlarged cardiac silhouette, a widened vascular pedicle, a prominent azygos vein, bilateral perihilar 'fluffy' consolidation with air bronchograms, and small bilateral pleural effusions. Which single finding on this same film would most strongly favor cardiogenic pulmonary edema over a primary bacterial pneumonia?
AThe presence of air bronchograms within the consolidation
BUnilateral, lobar distribution of the opacity
CA normal heart size
DThe combination of cardiomegaly, a widened vascular pedicle, and bilateral (rather than unilateral, lobar) distribution of the process
EThe presence of pleural fluid alone, since this never occurs in pneumonia
Explanation: Both heart failure and pneumonia can produce consolidation and even pleural fluid, which is why the two are often hard to distinguish on CXR. What tips the picture toward heart failure is the constellation of an enlarged heart, a widened vascular pedicle (reflecting distended central veins from volume overload), a prominent azygos vein, Kerley lines, and a symmetric, gravity-dependent, bilateral distribution — as opposed to the normal heart size, normal vascular pedicle, and typically unilateral, lobar consolidation of an uncomplicated bacterial pneumonia. Air bronchograms and pleural fluid, by themselves, can occur in either process.
Exam-style question
In interstitial pulmonary edema, where are Kerley B lines classically seen, and what do they represent?
AAs short (1–2 cm), horizontal lines perpendicular to the pleura near the costophrenic angles, representing fluid-distended peripheral interlobular septa
BIn the perihilar region, representing dilated central bronchi
CAt the lung apices, representing bullae
DAlong the trachea, representing tracheal deviation
EWithin the mediastinum, representing lymphadenopathy
Explanation: As pulmonary venous pressure rises further, fluid leaks beyond the central peribronchovascular interstitium into the thin interlobular septa at the lung periphery. Because these septa are oriented perpendicular to the pleural surface, the fluid-thickened septa appear as short (1–2 cm), horizontal white lines near the costophrenic angles — Kerley B lines. Fluid in the central peribronchovascular interstitium instead produces peribronchial cuffing (thickened bronchial walls in cross-section) and a hazy loss of definition of the hilar vessels ('perihilar haze').

Atypical and progressive pneumonias

Not every pneumonia looks like the dense, unilateral lobar consolidation of a typical bacterial infection. Certain organisms produce distinctive, and sometimes deceptively subtle, radiographic patterns.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae — the classic "atypical" pattern

A 12-year-old girl with mycoplasma pneumonia illustrates the classic atypical pattern: heterogeneous opacities involving both lungs symmetrically, with relative sparing of the lung apices — a distribution quite different from the unilateral, dense consolidation of typical bacterial pneumonia. On CT, mycoplasma pneumonia characteristically shows peribronchovascular ground-glass opacities with bronchial wall thickening, findings that are very commonly encountered in this infection and reflect its predilection for the airway walls and surrounding interstitium rather than pure airspace filling.

Legionella pneumophila — a pneumonia that progresses on imaging

Legionella pneumonia deserves special mention because, unlike most bacterial pneumonias, it can progress radiographically despite treatment over a very short time period. A 58-year-old man developed Legionella pneumonia after occupational exposure to a contaminated water source — he had been crawling through ventilation ducts at a refrigeration plant, a classic exposure route for Legionella, which thrives in stagnant water systems, cooling towers, and plumbing. His initial chest x-ray, obtained at symptom onset, showed a right infrahilar and basilar consolidation.

Just two days later, a repeat film in the same patient showed clear progression: enlargement of the right basilar consolidation, plus new consolidation appearing in the right upper lobe and in the periphery of the mid-left lung — findings consistent with rapid progression to multilobar, bilateral pneumonia. This tendency to spread quickly, even on treatment, is a recognized feature of Legionella and a useful clinical and radiographic clue when a pneumonia seems to be "getting worse" on serial films faster than expected.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
A 12-year-old girl has bilateral, symmetric, heterogeneous CXR opacities with relative sparing of the lung apices, and her chest CT shows peribronchovascular ground-glass opacity with bronchial wall thickening. Which organism is most classically associated with this pattern?
AStreptococcus pneumoniae (typical lobar pneumonia)
BLegionella pneumophila
CMycoplasma pneumoniae (an atypical pneumonia)
DMycobacterium tuberculosis
EPneumocystis jirovecii
Explanation: Mycoplasma pneumoniae classically produces an 'atypical' radiographic pattern in a young, otherwise healthy patient: bilateral, symmetric, heterogeneous opacities that spare the apices, with CT showing peribronchovascular ground-glass opacity and bronchial wall thickening rather than the dense, unilateral lobar consolidation of typical bacterial pneumonia.
Exam-style question
A 58-year-old man with occupational exposure to a contaminated water source (a refrigeration-plant vent) develops fever and dyspnea. His initial CXR shows a right infrahilar/basilar consolidation; two days later, a repeat film shows progression of that consolidation plus new consolidation in the right upper lobe and left mid-lung periphery. Which organism does this progression pattern most strongly suggest?
AMycoplasma pneumoniae
BPseudomonas aeruginosa (cavitary pneumonia)
CPneumocystis jirovecii
DInfluenza virus
ELegionella pneumophila
Explanation: Legionella pneumophila is acquired from contaminated water sources (cooling towers, plumbing, water-handling equipment) and classically causes a pneumonia that, unlike most typical bacterial pneumonias, tends to progress radiographically despite treatment — spreading from an initial unilateral basilar consolidation to multilobar and even contralateral involvement over just a few days, as illustrated here.

COPD on chest x-ray

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease produces a chest film that is often recognizable at a glance because of chronic hyperinflation and air trapping. On the frontal (PA) view, look for marked hyperinflation of both lungs: more than 10 posterior ribs may be counted above the diaphragm (11 in the example below), and the diaphragms appear flattened rather than their normal dome shape, a direct consequence of the lungs remaining over-expanded even at end-expiration.

The lateral view adds another clue: hyperinflation increases the retrosternal airspace — the space between the posterior sternum and the ascending aorta/anterior cardiac border — which enlarges as the overinflated lungs push the heart posteriorly and the diaphragm flattens.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
Which chest radiographic findings are classic for COPD/emphysema?
AA small, boot-shaped heart with reticular lower-lobe opacities
BHyperinflated lungs with 10 or more posterior ribs visible, flattened diaphragms, and an enlarged retrosternal airspace on the lateral view
CBilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with normal lung volumes
DA widened vascular pedicle with cephalization
EA lobar consolidation with air bronchograms
Explanation: Chronic airflow obstruction and loss of elastic recoil cause air trapping and hyperinflation: the lungs appear elongated and lucent, more than 10 posterior ribs may be counted above the diaphragm on a well-inspired film, and the diaphragms flatten (losing their normal dome shape). On the lateral view, hyperinflation increases the retrosternal airspace (the distance between the sternum and the ascending aorta/anterior heart border). None of the other choices describe the classic emphysematous chest.

Sarcoidosis: the four radiographic stages

Sarcoidosis, a multisystem granulomatous disease of uncertain cause, has a well-established radiographic staging system based on the appearance of the chest film. Each stage reflects a different balance between lymph node enlargement and parenchymal (lung tissue) involvement, and the stages often — though not invariably — represent a natural progression over time.

Stage 1: isolated hilar/mediastinal adenopathy

In Stage 1 sarcoidosis, the only radiographic abnormality is enlargement of the hilar and/or mediastinal lymph nodes, with clear lung parenchyma. This is often bilateral and symmetric.

Stage 2: adenopathy plus parenchymal disease

In Stage 2, the same nodal enlargement is now accompanied by parenchymal disease — infiltrates within the lung tissue itself, reflecting granulomatous involvement of the interstitium.

Stage 3: parenchymal disease without adenopathy

In Stage 3, the parenchymal infiltrates persist, but the lymphadenopathy that was present earlier has resolved — the disease burden has shifted from the nodes into the lung tissue itself.

Stage 4: pulmonary fibrosis (end-stage)

Stage 4 represents overt, established pulmonary fibrosis — the end result of chronic granulomatous inflammation, with architectural distortion, volume loss, and coarse fibrotic change (and often visible calcified granulomas), typically without significant residual adenopathy.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
A CXR shows bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymph node enlargement with clear lung parenchyma. According to the radiographic staging system for sarcoidosis, which stage is this?
AStage 0
BStage 2
CStage 3
DStage 1
EStage 4
Explanation: Sarcoidosis is staged radiographically by CXR appearance: Stage 1 is isolated hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy without parenchymal disease. Stage 2 adds parenchymal infiltrates alongside the adenopathy. Stage 3 shows parenchymal disease with the adenopathy having resolved. Stage 4 represents end-stage pulmonary fibrosis. (Stage 0 denotes a normal chest film despite biopsy-proven disease.)
Exam-style question
A sarcoidosis patient's CXR from several years ago showed hilar adenopathy plus reticulonodular infiltrates. Her current film shows architectural distortion, upper-lobe volume loss, and coarse fibrotic bands, with resolution of the previously seen adenopathy. What stage has she progressed to?
AStage 4 (fibrotic end-stage)
BStage 1
CStage 2
DStage 3
EThis represents disease regression, not progression
Explanation: Progression from Stage 2 (nodes + parenchymal infiltrates) through Stage 3 (parenchymal disease alone, nodes resolved) can culminate in Stage 4 disease: overt pulmonary fibrosis with architectural distortion, traction changes, and volume loss — the radiographic end stage of chronic granulomatous inflammation in sarcoidosis.

Pneumothorax and tension pneumothorax

Free air in the pleural space — pneumothorax — separates the visceral pleura from the chest wall and can occur spontaneously or from trauma. On CXR, look for a sharp white visceral pleural edge, with the space peripheral to that line appearing truly radiolucent because it lacks the normal branching vascular markings of aerated lung.

Recognizing pneumothorax: large and small examples

A large pneumothorax is usually obvious: this film shows a large left-sided pneumothorax, with an evident lack of lung markings on the left side compared to the normally aerated right side, and the collapsed lung visible retracted toward the hilum.

A smaller or more subtle pneumothorax requires closer inspection. This patient has a right-sided pneumothorax: the lung edge is marked by arrows, and there is a lack of vascular markings in the apex of the right lung compared to the fully aerated left lung. Also note the incidental right clavicle fracture — always review the bones on every chest film, since fractures can point toward the mechanism and severity of an underlying injury.

The expiratory view trick

In the same patient, an expiratory view was obtained, and it enhances the pneumothorax: because the volume of free pleural air does not change between inspiration and expiration but the lung itself becomes smaller on expiration, the pneumothorax now occupies proportionally more of the hemithorax, making the lung edge easier to see. The lack of vessel markings in the apex is still present, the clavicle fracture remains visible, and the contralateral (left) lung remains normal for comparison.

Tension pneumothorax: a clinical emergency

When a pneumothorax is large enough that intrapleural pressure rises and shifts the mediastinum away from the affected side, obstructing venous return to the heart and causing hypotension, this is termed a tension pneumothorax — a true medical emergency that is diagnosed clinically (absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation, hypotension) and treated immediately with needle decompression or chest tube placement, without waiting for confirmatory imaging if the presentation is convincing.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
On an upright CXR, which finding confirms a pneumothorax?
AA meniscus-shaped opacity at the costophrenic angle
BBilateral perihilar haze with Kerley B lines
CA sharp white visceral pleural line, with absence of normal lung markings in the space peripheral to that line
DFlattening of the diaphragm with 11 visible posterior ribs
EWidening of the vascular pedicle
Explanation: Air in the pleural space separates the visceral pleura from the chest wall. The visceral pleural edge appears as a thin, sharp white line, and the space between that line and the chest wall lacks the normal branching vascular markings of aerated lung (it is truly radiolucent, containing only free air). In a small pneumothorax, this line can be subtle and mistaken for a rib margin; an expiratory film increases the pneumothorax's relative volume and makes the pleural line easier to identify.
Exam-style question
A trauma patient develops sudden hypotension and a large right pneumothorax with the trachea and mediastinum visibly shifted to the left on CXR. What is this presentation called, and what is the immediate management?
ASimple pneumothorax; observation and repeat film in 6 hours
BHemothorax; urgent thoracotomy
CFlail chest; positive-pressure ventilation
DPneumomediastinum; conservative management
ETension pneumothorax; emergent needle decompression (or chest tube), not confirmatory imaging first
Explanation: When intrapleural pressure from a pneumothorax rises high enough to shift the mediastinum away from the affected side and obstruct venous return to the heart, the result is a tension pneumothorax — a clinical diagnosis and a true emergency. Treatment is emergent decompression (needle decompression or chest tube) based on the physical exam findings (absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation, hypotension); one should not wait for a confirmatory chest x-ray if the presentation is convincing, since the delay can be fatal.
Exam-style question
Why is an expiratory chest film sometimes obtained when a small pneumothorax is suspected but not clearly seen on a standard inspiratory film?
AExpiration increases lung volume, making the pneumothorax harder to see
BExpiration decreases the lung's volume while the pleural air volume stays fixed, so the pneumothorax occupies a relatively larger share of the hemithorax and its edge becomes easier to identify
CExpiratory views eliminate motion artifact from the heart
DExpiratory views are required to see Kerley B lines
EExpiratory views are only used to assess diaphragmatic excursion
Explanation: The absolute volume of free pleural air does not change between inspiration and expiration, but the lung itself becomes smaller in expiration. This makes the pneumothorax proportionally larger relative to the shrunken lung and the visceral pleural line stand out more clearly against the chest wall — a simple trick for confirming a subtle pneumothorax at the bedside.

Trauma: rib fractures, subcutaneous emphysema, and spine injury

Trauma to the chest wall frequently produces findings well beyond the lung parenchyma, and a systematic review of the bones and soft tissues is essential on every trauma chest film.

Rib fractures and subcutaneous emphysema

This patient sustained multiple rib fractures along with subcutaneous air tracking through the soft tissues of the chest wall, shoulder, and neck — subcutaneous emphysema. This finding typically indicates that air has escaped from an injured lung or an underlying pneumothorax into the surrounding tissue planes, and its presence — especially alongside multiple rib fractures — should prompt a deliberate search for an associated pneumothorax, hemothorax, or pulmonary laceration on that same film or on a follow-up CT.

Thoracic spine compression fractures

Bony injury is not limited to the ribs. A lateral chest film in another patient demonstrates compression fractures at the T6–T8 and T9 vertebral levels — a reminder that the lateral view, often obtained primarily to assess the lungs and retrosternal space, can also be the key to identifying vertebral compression fractures that might otherwise be missed if attention is confined to the lung fields alone.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
A CXR obtained after blunt chest trauma shows multiple rib fractures and lucent streaks of air tracking through the soft tissues of the chest wall, shoulder, and neck. What does this soft-tissue finding represent, and why does it matter?
APneumomediastinum from esophageal rupture only
BNormal skin fold artifact
CCalcified costal cartilage
DSubcutaneous emphysema — air dissecting through the soft tissues, usually from an underlying pneumothorax or lacerated lung — and it should prompt a careful search for an associated pneumothorax
EA rib fracture callus from a healed injury
Explanation: Air tracking through the subcutaneous soft tissues (subcutaneous emphysema) most often signals an underlying pneumothorax or parenchymal lung injury that is allowing air to escape into the tissue planes. Its presence — especially with multiple rib fractures, which raise the likelihood of an underlying pleural or lung injury — should prompt a deliberate search on the CXR (and, if needed, CT) for a coexisting pneumothorax, hemothorax, or pulmonary laceration, since the fractures themselves are a marker of the force involved.
Exam-style question
Beyond the lung fields, which structures should be systematically reviewed on every chest radiograph, particularly after trauma?
AThe bones (ribs, spine, clavicles, scapulae), soft tissues, cardiac/mediastinal silhouette, diaphragm, and any monitoring equipment or lines/tubes
BOnly the lung parenchyma; bones and soft tissues are assessed on CT alone
COnly the diaphragm and costophrenic angles
DOnly the airway and great vessels
EOnly areas where the patient reports pain
Explanation: A systematic 'ABCDEF' review of the chest film — Airway, Bones/breast shadows, Cardiac silhouette/mediastinum, Diaphragm/upper abdomen, Equipment (lines, tubes, devices), and Fields of the lungs — ensures that findings outside the lung parenchyma are not missed. In trauma this is especially important: a lateral view demonstrating compression fractures of the thoracic vertebrae, or a frontal view showing a clavicle fracture or rib fractures, may be the only clue to the mechanism and severity of injury, and matters just as much as the lung findings themselves.

Central lines, endotracheal tubes, and gastric tubes

One of the most frequent reasons a portable chest film is ordered in the hospital, especially in the ICU, is to confirm the position of monitoring and support devices: central venous catheters, endotracheal tubes, and gastric (naso- or orogastric) tubes. This patient, who also has patchy bilateral infiltrates, has all three devices in place.

When the same film is annotated, the three devices can be traced individually: the central line (blue) courses through the right internal jugular/subclavian system down to a good position near the cavoatrial junction; the endotracheal tube (yellow) sits appropriately above the carina; and the gastric tube (green) courses down the esophagus and curls within the stomach, well below the diaphragm — all in good position.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
In a critically ill patient with a portable AP chest film showing a central venous catheter, an endotracheal tube, and a nasogastric/orogastric tube, what constitutes 'good position' for each device on CXR?
ACentral line tip in the right atrium; ETT tip at the carina; gastric tube tip in the esophagus
BAll three tubes should overlap the cardiac silhouette
CCentral line tip near the cavoatrial junction/lower SVC; ETT tip roughly 3–5 cm above the carina; gastric tube tip below the diaphragm within the stomach
DETT tip in the right mainstem bronchus is preferred for better right lung ventilation
ECentral line and gastric tube positions cannot be assessed on a chest film
Explanation: Line and tube position is one of the most common reasons a CXR is ordered in the ICU. A properly positioned central venous catheter tip sits near the cavoatrial junction (lower SVC), avoiding the atrium; a well-placed endotracheal tube tip sits several centimeters above the carina (too low risks mainstem intubation, too high risks accidental extubation); and a gastric tube's tip should be seen clearly below the diaphragm within the gastric bubble, confirming it has not curled back into the esophagus or entered the airway.

Diffuse parenchymal (interstitial) lung disease on CT

When interstitial lung disease is suspected, high-resolution CT — thin-slice imaging reconstructed with a high spatial-frequency algorithm — is far more sensitive than plain CXR for characterizing the pattern and distribution of disease, and different diseases produce recognizably different CT signatures.

Usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP / idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis)

A patient with usual interstitial pneumonia shows honeycombing and fibrotic change concentrated at the lung bases and along the periphery (subpleural), with areas of relatively normal-appearing lung visible above the honeycombing. This patchy alternation between fibrotic and normal-appearing lung — spatial and temporal heterogeneity — is a defining feature of the UIP pattern, distinguishing it from the more uniform ground-glass processes discussed below.

COVID-19 pneumonia

A CT scan of a patient with COVID-19 pneumonia shows ground-glass infiltrates that are predominantly peripheral in location — a pattern that became a widely recognized hallmark during the pandemic, though it is not perfectly specific to this virus and can be mimicked by other viral or organizing pneumonias.

Pseudomonas (cavitary/necrotizing) pneumonia

A 64-year-old woman with Pseudomonas pneumonia demonstrates a very different appearance: an area of consolidation with cavity formation — a gas- or fluid-filled space within the consolidated lung, reflecting the necrotizing, tissue-destructive potential of this organism (shared by other necrotizing bacterial pathogens such as Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella, and anaerobes).

Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP)

This scan shows nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, with some pleural/subpleural interstitial prominence most pronounced in both lower lobes, associated with traction bronchiectasis (airway dilation from surrounding fibrotic traction). NSIP tends to be more uniform in distribution than UIP, without the discrete honeycombing that characterizes UIP.

Desquamative interstitial pneumonia (DIP)

A 64-year-old man with a 17-year history of tobacco use presented with desquamative interstitial pneumonia — a smoking-related interstitial lung disease. Imaging shows small cysts in both lower lobes with surrounding interstitial prominence, a pattern related to (but distinct from) the ground-glass pattern of respiratory bronchiolitis-associated interstitial lung disease seen in other smokers.

Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP)

A 43-year-old man with a history of follicular lymphoma, who had undergone chemotherapy and was admitted for respiratory failure, demonstrated predominantly peripheral ground-glass opacities. Lung biopsy yielded organizing pneumonia — granulation tissue plugging the distal airspaces and alveolar ducts. The patient did well on corticosteroids and was discharged home, illustrating the marked steroid-responsiveness that is characteristic of this entity (whether cryptogenic, as the name implies when no cause is found, or secondary to an identifiable trigger like chemotherapy, as here).

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis

A 28-year-old woman presented with cough, shortness of breath, and dyspnea on exertion. She lived at home with her sister, who owned an African grey parrot — a key exposure clue, since hypersensitivity pneumonitis is an immune-mediated reaction to a repeatedly inhaled organic antigen (classically avian proteins, but also molds and other organic dusts). Imaging showed widespread ground-glass opacity with hypoattenuation and hypovascularity of scattered secondary pulmonary lobules — a mosaic pattern reflecting small-airway involvement. Her clinical symptoms worsened with continued exposure, supporting the diagnosis.

Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP)

A 41-year-old woman presented with approximately six months of shortness of breath and dry cough, now with continued dyspnea. Axial and coronal CT scans show a "crazy-paving" appearance — geographic ground-glass opacity with superimposed smooth interlobular septal thickening, resembling irregular paving stones. Bronchoscopy with biopsy confirmed pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, a disease in which surfactant-derived lipoproteinaceous material accumulates within the alveoli.

Comparative summary of the diffuse parenchymal patterns

DiseaseClassic CT patternDistributionKey clinical clue
UIP / IPFHoneycombing, patchy fibrosisSubpleural, basal, heterogeneous (normal lung interspersed)Chronic, progressive dyspnea, often idiopathic or age-related
COVID-19 pneumoniaGround-glass opacityPeripheral, bilateralAcute viral illness, exposure/pandemic context
Pseudomonas / necrotizing pneumoniaConsolidation with cavitationFocalSevere/nosocomial bacterial infection
NSIPGround-glass + traction bronchiectasis, no honeycombingBibasilar, more uniform than UIPOften connective-tissue disease-associated
DIPGround-glass with small cystsBibasilarHeavy smoking history
COPPatchy ground-glass/consolidationPeripheral/peribronchialSteroid-responsive; cryptogenic or secondary (chemo, infection)
Hypersensitivity pneumonitisGround-glass, mosaic ("head-cheese") patternDiffuseRepeated organic antigen exposure (birds, mold, hay)
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis"Crazy paving" (ground-glass + septal thickening)Geographic, diffuseConfirmed by bronchoscopic lavage/biopsy

Check yourself

Exam-style question
A high-resolution CT in a patient with usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP/IPF) shows subpleural, basal-predominant honeycombing with normal-appearing lung interspersed among fibrotic areas. What does 'honeycombing' represent, and what is its typical distribution in UIP?
ADiffuse ground-glass opacity with no cystic change, distributed centrally
BA single large bulla at the apex
CMiliary nodules scattered randomly throughout both lungs
DSmooth interlobular septal thickening without cyst formation
EClustered subpleural cystic airspaces with thick fibrotic walls, patchy and predominantly basal/peripheral, alternating with areas of relatively normal lung
Explanation: Honeycombing refers to clusters of small, thick-walled cystic airspaces that form as chronically inflamed, fibrotic lung remodels itself. In usual interstitial pneumonia — the pathologic/radiologic pattern underlying idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis — this honeycombing is characteristically patchy (temporally and spatially heterogeneous) and concentrated at the lung bases and periphery (subpleural), with areas of relatively preserved, normal-appearing lung interspersed between fibrotic zones — a key distinguishing feature from other interstitial pneumonias, which tend to be more uniform.
Exam-style question
A patient with acute respiratory illness has a chest CT showing bilateral ground-glass opacities that are predominantly peripheral and subpleural in distribution. In the appropriate clinical context, this pattern is most classically described in which condition?
AUsual interstitial pneumonia (UIP)
BCOVID-19 pneumonia
CSimple pneumothorax
DSarcoidosis stage 1
EPulmonary alveolar proteinosis
Explanation: COVID-19 pneumonia classically produces bilateral, multifocal ground-glass opacities with a peripheral and subpleural predominance on chest CT, often most pronounced in the lower lobes — a pattern that, while not perfectly specific, became a hallmark imaging clue during the pandemic and remains a classic teaching example of a viral pneumonia's CT appearance.
Exam-style question
A 64-year-old woman's chest CT shows a focal area of consolidation with a cavity (air-fluid level) within it. Which organism is classically associated with cavitary, necrotizing pneumonia of this kind?
AMycoplasma pneumoniae
BRespiratory syncytial virus
CChlamydia pneumoniae
DPseudomonas aeruginosa
ERhinovirus
Explanation: Certain necrotizing bacterial organisms — classically Pseudomonas aeruginosa, along with Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and anaerobes — can destroy lung tissue fast enough to produce cavitation (an air- or fluid-filled space) within an area of consolidation, a finding not typically seen with atypical organisms like Mycoplasma or with most viral pneumonias.
Exam-style question
A 41-year-old woman with six months of dyspnea and dry cough has a CT showing diffuse ground-glass opacity with superimposed smooth interlobular septal thickening, producing a 'crazy-paving' appearance; bronchoscopic biopsy confirms the diagnosis. Which disease does this describe?
APulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP)
BUsual interstitial pneumonia
CHypersensitivity pneumonitis
DCryptogenic organizing pneumonia
EDesquamative interstitial pneumonia
Explanation: 'Crazy paving' — geographic ground-glass opacity with superimposed smooth septal and intralobular line thickening, resembling irregularly shaped paving stones — is the classic CT description of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, a disease in which surfactant-derived lipoproteinaceous material accumulates within the alveoli. It also can be seen (less classically) in some infections and adenocarcinomas, but PAP is the textbook association, and bronchoscopic lavage/biopsy is used to confirm it.
Exam-style question
A 43-year-old man with a history of follicular lymphoma undergoing chemotherapy develops respiratory failure. CT shows predominantly peripheral ground-glass opacities, and lung biopsy reveals organizing pneumonia within the alveolar ducts and airspaces. He improves markedly on corticosteroids. Which diagnosis fits best?
AUsual interstitial pneumonia
BPulmonary alveolar proteinosis
CCryptogenic (or secondary) organizing pneumonia
DLegionella pneumonia
EEmphysema
Explanation: Organizing pneumonia is characterized histologically by plugs of granulation tissue filling the distal airspaces and alveolar ducts, and on CT by patchy, often peripheral or peribronchial ground-glass opacities and consolidations. When no clear trigger is found it is termed cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP); when a cause such as chemotherapy, infection, or connective tissue disease is identified, it is secondary organizing pneumonia. Both forms are notably steroid-responsive, as seen here.
Exam-style question
A 28-year-old woman develops cough and dyspnea after moving in with her sister, whose home has an African grey parrot. CT shows widespread ground-glass opacity with hypoattenuating, hypovascular areas ('head-cheese' pattern), and her symptoms worsen with continued exposure. Which diagnosis is most likely, and what is the key exposure history clue?
AUsual interstitial pneumonia, unrelated to any exposure
BCryptogenic organizing pneumonia, triggered by chemotherapy
CPulmonary alveolar proteinosis, triggered by silica dust
DLegionella pneumonia, triggered by contaminated water
EHypersensitivity pneumonitis, triggered by inhaled avian (bird-related) antigens
Explanation: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is an immune-mediated lung reaction to a repeatedly inhaled antigen — classically avian proteins (bird fancier's/breeder's lung), but also molds, hay dust, and other organic antigens. The clinical clue is almost always an exposure history, as in this case with a household parrot; CT shows widespread ground-glass opacity, often with a mosaic ('head-cheese') pattern of hypoattenuating, hypovascular lobules reflecting small-airway involvement, and symptoms characteristically worsen with continued or repeated exposure.

Point-of-care lung ultrasound

Ultrasound has become an increasingly useful tool in pulmonary diagnosis. It can be performed rapidly at the bedside, requires no ionizing radiation or contrast, and is often obtained even before a formal CXR when a disease must be managed promptly — such as suspected pneumothorax or a large-volume pleural effusion.

Occult rib fracture

This patient had an extremely subtle rib fracture that was not clearly appreciated on the plain chest film. Bedside ultrasound, however, clearly demonstrated the rib fracture along with an adjacent hematoma — ultrasound's high-frequency resolution of the bone cortex makes a fracture step-off, and the associated soft-tissue hematoma, often easier to identify than on a subtle plain radiograph.

Ultrasound in pleural effusion and pneumonia

Ultrasound is most commonly used to diagnose pleural effusions or pneumothorax at the bedside. Pleural effusions are visualized as a fluid hyperdensity (anechoic-to-hypoechoic collection) above the diaphragm, and ultrasound can help guide management — including placement of chest tubes for drainage and identification of highly viscous effusions that may instead require surgical treatment.

While ultrasound has historically been used less for nonpleural lung disorders, emerging evidence shows it can also be useful in diagnosing severe pneumonias, such as those seen in COVID-19. An experienced sonographer can detect subtle abnormalities in the interference patterns of sound waves reverberating off lung affected by pneumonia. In severe disease, widened B-lines become so numerous and closely packed that they create a cascading "waterfall sign," reflecting extensive interstitial and alveolar involvement.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
A patient with an extremely subtle rib fracture that was not clearly visualized on CXR is evaluated with bedside ultrasound. What can ultrasound demonstrate in this setting that a plain film may miss?
ANothing additional; ultrasound cannot assess bone
BA cortical step-off/discontinuity at the fracture site along with an adjacent soft-tissue hematoma
CThe precise Wells score for pulmonary embolism
DHoneycombing in the adjacent lung
EThe artery-to-bronchus ratio
Explanation: High-frequency ultrasound is excellent at resolving the bone cortex as a bright, continuous line; a fracture appears as a step-off or discontinuity in that cortical line, often with an adjacent hypoechoic hematoma — findings that can be more conspicuous at the bedside with ultrasound than on a subtle plain radiograph, particularly for rib fractures that are easily obscured by overlapping structures on CXR.
Exam-style question
On lung ultrasound, how does a pleural effusion typically appear, and where is it best sought?
AAs a hyperechoic (bright), solid-appearing mass within the lung parenchyma itself
BAs a bright, sharp line with no deeper structures visible, at the lung apex
CAs a rapidly oscillating comet-tail artifact throughout both lung fields
DAs an anechoic-to-hypoechoic fluid collection above the diaphragm, between the chest wall/lung and the liver or spleen, best sought in the dependent (gravity-influenced) recess
EUltrasound cannot detect pleural fluid; only CT can
Explanation: Pleural fluid is anechoic to hypoechoic (dark) on ultrasound and is best identified in the dependent recess just above the diaphragm, seen as a fluid collection between the lung/chest wall and the underlying liver (right) or spleen (left). Because it requires no radiation or contrast and can be performed instantly at the bedside, ultrasound is a fast, sensitive way to confirm and even guide drainage of a pleural effusion, particularly when a large-volume effusion needs urgent bedside diagnosis.
Exam-style question
In a patient with suspected severe COVID-19 pneumonia, what lung ultrasound finding has been described as the 'waterfall sign,' and what does it reflect?
AMultiple, closely packed, widened B-lines that resemble a cascading waterfall, reflecting diffuse interstitial/alveolar involvement from severe pneumonia
BA single, isolated A-line, reflecting normally aerated lung
CA meniscus sign, reflecting pleural effusion
DLung sliding, reflecting normal visceral-parietal pleural apposition
EA bare cortical line, reflecting an occult rib fracture
Explanation: Normal, well-aerated lung reflects ultrasound waves as discrete horizontal A-lines. As interstitial and alveolar disease worsens — as in severe pneumonia including COVID-19 — the number and width of the vertical B-lines (arising from thickened, fluid-laden interlobular septa reaching the pleural surface) increases dramatically, and when they become confluent and closely packed they create a cascading appearance likened to a waterfall. An experienced sonographer can pick up this pattern of severe parenchymal involvement quickly at the bedside.

Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scanning

A ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan is a nuclear medicine study most commonly used to assess the likelihood of pulmonary embolism when other diagnostic tests are not an option — for example, when a patient has severe renal insufficiency, has had a severe allergic reaction to iodinated contrast media, or cannot tolerate the radiation dose of a CT pulmonary angiogram (a consideration in some pregnant patients).

The scan works by administering radioactive tracers separately for perfusion (injected intravenously, distributing through the pulmonary circulation) and ventilation (inhaled, distributing through the airways). A normal scan shows the same pattern of ventilation and perfusion throughout the lung, since all aerated lung is normally also perfused. When a segment of lung ventilates normally but fails to perfuse, this V/Q mismatch is the classic signature of pulmonary embolism: the thrombus has obstructed blood flow to that segment without affecting the patency of its airways.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
In which clinical scenarios is a ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan preferred over CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) for evaluating suspected pulmonary embolism?
AIn every patient, since V/Q scanning is always more accurate than CTPA
BOnly in pediatric patients
CIn patients with severe renal insufficiency, a history of severe contrast allergy, or an inability to tolerate the radiation dose of CTPA (eg, some pregnant patients)
DOnly when the D-dimer is markedly elevated
ENever; V/Q scanning has been entirely replaced by CTPA
Explanation: CTPA is generally the first-line, most sensitive and specific single test for pulmonary embolism, but it requires iodinated contrast (a problem in significant renal insufficiency or severe contrast allergy) and involves a certain radiation dose. V/Q scanning serves as the key alternative in patients who cannot safely undergo CTPA for one of these reasons, since the nuclear medicine ventilation and perfusion agents avoid iodinated contrast and can be used in a lower-radiation protocol appropriate for some pregnant patients.
Exam-style question
A V/Q scan shows normal, matched ventilation and perfusion throughout both lungs except for a segment in the left lower lobe that ventilates normally but does not perfuse. How should this mismatch be interpreted?
AAs a normal variant requiring no further workup
BAs evidence against pulmonary embolism, since perfusion defects rule out PE
CAs evidence of COPD with air trapping
DAs evidence of pneumonia in that segment
EAs a ventilation-perfusion mismatch consistent with pulmonary embolism — a segment that moves air normally but lacks blood flow, as would occur with a thrombus obstructing that segment's pulmonary artery branch
Explanation: The physiologic logic of the V/Q scan is straightforward: an embolus blocks blood flow (perfusion) to the lung segment(s) downstream of the clot without necessarily affecting that segment's ability to move air in and out (ventilation), since the airways themselves remain patent. A segment that ventilates normally but fails to perfuse is therefore a mismatched defect and the classic V/Q signature of pulmonary embolism, in contrast to pneumonia or other airway disease, which tends to produce matched ventilation and perfusion defects in the same location.

CT pulmonary angiography and PET/CT

CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA)

CT pulmonary angiography uses intravenously injected radiocontrast to delineate the pulmonary vascular system with cross-sectional CT, making it the modality of choice for diseases of the pulmonary arteries and veins — most importantly pulmonary embolism, as well as aortic dissection. After the contrast bolus reaches the pulmonary arteries, the CT is performed, and a thrombus appears as a filling defect within the contrast-opacified vessel.

The example below shows a large saddle embolus — a thrombus that straddles the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery into the right and left branches. Because a saddle embolus threatens blood flow to both lungs simultaneously, it carries a substantially higher risk of acute right ventricular strain, hemodynamic compromise, and sudden death than a smaller, more peripheral embolus, and is treated as a high-risk finding warranting close monitoring.

Clinical pearlRecently, MRI has been found to be equally effective as CTPA in diagnosing pulmonary emboli, with the advantage of avoiding both iodinated contrast and ionizing radiation — an option worth knowing about for patients in whom both CT and V/Q scanning are problematic.

PET/CT

A PET/CT scan is a functional imaging technique that uses radioactive biomarkers — typically a glucose analog — to detect tissue with abnormally high metabolic activity, superimposed on the anatomic detail of a CT scan. In chest imaging, PET/CT is used mostly to detect and stage lung tumors and to assess the extent of cancer metastasis within the lung and elsewhere in the body. It is also useful for monitoring treatment response: a tumor responding well to therapy will show a marked reduction in tracer uptake, sometimes before any change in size is visible on CT.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
A CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrates a large filling defect straddling the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery into the right and left pulmonary arteries. What is this specific finding called, and why is it clinically significant?
AA 'Hampton's hump,' a benign finding requiring no intervention
BA 'saddle embolus,' a large central thrombus at the main pulmonary artery bifurcation that carries a high risk of hemodynamic compromise and right heart strain
CA 'crazy-paving' pattern, indicating pulmonary alveolar proteinosis
DA 'tree-in-bud' pattern, indicating endobronchial spread of infection
EAn 'air crescent sign,' indicating a fungal cavity
Explanation: A thrombus that lodges at the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery — straddling both the right and left pulmonary artery origins — is called a saddle embolus. Because it obstructs flow to both lungs simultaneously (or threatens to), a saddle embolus carries a substantially higher risk of acute right ventricular strain, hemodynamic instability, and sudden death than a smaller, more peripheral embolus, and is considered a high-risk finding warranting close hemodynamic monitoring and consideration of more aggressive therapy.
Exam-style question
What is the primary chest-imaging application of a PET/CT scan, and how does it work?
AIt directly visualizes thrombus within the pulmonary arteries using iodinated contrast
BIt is the first-line study for diagnosing pneumothorax
CIt measures ventilation and perfusion matching, replacing V/Q scanning
DIt uses radioactive biomarkers (most often a glucose analog) to detect tissue with abnormally high metabolic activity, and is mainly used to detect and stage lung tumors and assess treatment response
EIt is primarily used to diagnose interstitial lung disease
Explanation: PET/CT combines functional imaging (positron emission tomography, using a radioactive tracer — typically a glucose analog that concentrates in metabolically hyperactive tissue) with the anatomic detail of CT. In the chest, its dominant use is oncologic: detecting primary lung tumors, assessing nodal and distant metastatic spread for staging, and monitoring response to treatments such as chemotherapy, since a tumor that responds well will show a marked reduction in tracer uptake even before its size on CT has changed.

Lung nodules and lung cancer screening

A lung nodule identified incidentally on chest x-ray is generally further characterized with a dedicated chest CT, which provides far more detail than the two-dimensional radiograph: precise measurement, assessment of margins and internal density (solid versus part-solid versus ground-glass; calcification or fat favoring a benign etiology; spiculated margins or cavitation raising concern for malignancy), and a survey of the rest of the lung for additional nodules.

Low-dose CT lung cancer screening

Current guidance recommends annual screening for lung cancer with low-dose computed tomography in adults who fall within a defined age range and who have an extensive cumulative smoking history (measured in pack-years) and either currently smoke or have quit within roughly the past 15 years. Screening is generally discontinued once a person has not smoked for about 15 years, or if they develop a health problem that substantially limits life expectancy or the ability or willingness to undergo curative lung surgery, since the benefit of early detection depends on the patient remaining a viable candidate for definitive treatment. (Exact age range and pack-year thresholds have been revised over time by professional guideline bodies — always confirm the currently active criteria before counseling a patient.)

Check yourself

Exam-style question
A lung nodule identified on chest x-ray is further characterized with a dedicated chest CT. Why is CT generally superior to CXR for evaluating a solitary pulmonary nodule?
ACT provides cross-sectional detail that allows precise measurement, assessment of margins/density (eg, calcification, fat, cavitation), and detection of additional nodules not visible on the two-dimensional chest film
BCT cannot show pulmonary nodules at all
CCT eliminates the need for any tissue biopsy in every case
DCXR always shows nodules better because it has higher resolution than CT
ECT is preferred only because it uses less radiation than CXR
Explanation: A two-dimensional chest radiograph can only show a nodule as a single silhouette, superimposed on overlying ribs, vessels, and soft tissue, which limits characterization. Cross-sectional CT allows the nodule to be measured precisely, its margins and internal density evaluated (solid vs part-solid vs ground-glass; calcification or fat suggesting a benign process; spiculation or cavitation raising concern for malignancy), and the rest of the lung surveyed for additional nodules — information essential for risk-stratifying the finding and deciding on follow-up imaging versus biopsy.
Exam-style question
According to current lung cancer screening guidance, which patient is an appropriate candidate for annual low-dose CT screening?
AA 40-year-old with a 10-pack-year smoking history who quit 20 years ago
BAny adult over age 80, regardless of smoking history
CA 65-year-old with a substantial (eg, 20+ pack-year) smoking history who currently smokes, or who quit within the past 15 years, and who falls within the guideline-specified age range
DA never-smoker with a family history of lung cancer
EA 50-year-old who has never smoked but has occupational asbestos exposure only
Explanation: Low-dose CT lung cancer screening is targeted at adults within a defined age range who have a substantial cumulative smoking history and either currently smoke or quit within roughly the last 15 years — reflecting the population in whom the mortality benefit of early detection has been demonstrated to outweigh the risks of radiation exposure and false-positive findings. Screening is generally stopped once a person has been smoke-free for about 15 years, or if a health problem develops that would preclude curative treatment even if cancer were found. (Consult current USPSTF guidance for the exact age range and pack-year threshold in effect, as these figures have been revised over time.)

Case connection: the patient who couldn't breathe

Vignette"He's having so much trouble breathing. Please help us." This begins your conversation with TD's wife as she brings her husband into the emergency department. TD is a tall, thin 22-year-old patient presenting with acute, severe shortness of breath. TD has no prior medical history of breathing issues. On exam, the patient is afebrile, his respirations are 28 breaths/min and shallow, his heart rate is 94 beats/min, and his blood pressure is 128/70 mmHg. On examination of his lungs, you cannot hear breath sounds on the left. "Let's look at that chest x-ray right now," the emergency department attending tells you. "I am concerned about a pneumothorax."

Applying the systematic ABCDEF approach to TD's chest film: his trachea (A) is deviated to the right. His bones, cardiac shadow, and diaphragm (B-C-D) are otherwise normal, though the mediastinum is slightly shifted to the right. He has no devices (E) in his chest or chest wall. When you examine the lung fields (F), you notice a sharp white linear shadow of the visceral pleura on the left, with no normal lung markings peripheral to that shadow.

Putting the exam and the film together: a tall, thin young man (a classic body habitus for primary spontaneous pneumothorax), absent breath sounds on the left, a deviated trachea, and a visceral pleural line with an absent peripheral vascular pattern on CXR — this is a pneumothorax, and given the tracheal/mediastinal shift, a tension pneumothorax. An emergency needle decompression is performed by the attending; air is released, and the patient immediately improves. TD is admitted for continued observation.

Clinical pearl"The physical exam and the chest x-ray made the diagnosis," the attending says during the end-of-shift debriefing. "Nothing fancy at all." A bedside ultrasound, used quickly in a patient like TD, would also have been expected to suggest pneumothorax even before the formal film was reviewed — reinforcing that the fastest, most available tools (a careful exam, a systematic film review, and point-of-care ultrasound) are often exactly what a life-threatening diagnosis like tension pneumothorax requires.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
A 22-year-old previously healthy man presents with acute, severe shortness of breath. He is afebrile, tachypneic (28/min, shallow), with a heart rate of 94 and blood pressure of 128/70. Breath sounds are absent on the left. The attending suspects pneumothorax. Using the ABCDEF systematic CXR review, which finding would most directly support this diagnosis before any imaging is even obtained?
AWheezing on auscultation of the right lung
BA prolonged expiratory phase bilaterally
CBilateral crackles at both lung bases
DA pericardial friction rub
ETracheal deviation and absent breath sounds on the affected side, which on a subsequent CXR would correspond to a deviated trachea/mediastinum (A) and a sharp visceral pleural line with absent lung markings peripheral to it (F, fields)
Explanation: The physical exam (absent breath sounds unilaterally, and in a tension physiology, tracheal deviation away from the affected side) can strongly suggest pneumothorax even before imaging. Confirmatory CXR, reviewed systematically, would show the airway (trachea) deviated away from the affected side, and the lung fields would show the telltale sharp white visceral pleural line with the peripheral space beyond it lacking normal vascular markings — precisely the findings expected in a large or tension pneumothorax.
Exam-style question
In the case above, if the patient's blood pressure had dropped and his trachea were visibly deviated to the right on exam, what would this suggest, and what should happen next?
ASimple pneumothorax; wait for a formal chest x-ray before any intervention
BTension pneumothorax on the left, causing mediastinal shift and impaired venous return; emergent needle decompression should not be delayed for imaging
CA large pleural effusion; thoracentesis should be scheduled electively
DBilateral pneumothorax; no urgent action is needed
EA normal finding in a healthy 22-year-old
Explanation: Hypotension accompanying tracheal deviation away from a pneumothorax is the clinical signature of a tension pneumothorax — rising intrapleural pressure on the affected side pushes the mediastinum toward the opposite side and kinks/compresses the great veins, impairing venous return and cardiac output. This is a life-threatening emergency, and treatment (needle decompression, followed by chest tube placement) must proceed immediately based on the clinical picture rather than waiting for confirmatory imaging.

Imaging modality quick-reference

ModalityWhat it's best forKey limitation(s)
Chest x-ray (CXR)First-line study for nearly all respiratory complaints; consolidation, interstitial patterns, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, line/tube position, bony injuryTwo-dimensional (superimposition of structures); limited sensitivity for subtle interstitial disease and small pneumothoraces
CT scan (incl. high-resolution CT)Detailed characterization of parenchymal disease, nodules/masses, interstitial lung disease patterns, bronchial wall thickeningHigher radiation dose than CXR; usually requires the patient to lie still/breath-hold
CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA)The single best test for pulmonary embolism when contrast can be given safely; also aortic dissectionRequires iodinated contrast — problematic with severe renal insufficiency or contrast allergy
Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scanAlternative to CTPA for suspected PE when contrast/radiation cannot be used (severe renal disease, contrast allergy, some pregnant patients)Lower specificity than CTPA in patients with underlying lung disease (matched defects can obscure a mismatch)
PET/CTDetecting and staging lung tumors/metastases; assessing treatment responseNot useful for acute processes like pneumothorax or PE; false positives from inflammation/infection
UltrasoundRapid bedside diagnosis of pneumothorax and pleural effusion; can also detect occult rib fractures and, increasingly, severe pneumonia (eg, COVID-19)Operator-dependent; limited by body habitus, chest wall dressings, and overlying air/bone
MRIEmerging alternative to CTPA for PE, avoiding both contrast and radiationLimited availability, longer acquisition time, not yet first-line

Check yourself

Exam-style question
Which imaging modality is generally considered the single best test for diagnosing pulmonary embolism in a patient who can safely receive iodinated contrast?
AChest x-ray (PA and lateral)
BVentilation/perfusion scan
CLung ultrasound
DCT pulmonary angiography (CTPA)
EPET/CT
Explanation: CTPA directly visualizes the pulmonary arterial tree after contrast injection and can identify a thrombus as a filling defect with excellent sensitivity and specificity, making it the preferred, first-line test for pulmonary embolism whenever the patient's renal function and contrast tolerance allow it. V/Q scanning, ultrasound, and plain CXR each play supporting or alternative roles but are not the primary diagnostic test for PE.
